AI is rapidly reshaping the administrative side of Laundry And Dry Cleaning Workers, but people still carry the core skills and interpersonal work. This guide breaks down the impact and practical responses.
It does not suit people who dislike dirt, repetition, or persistent stains. Laundry work is often damp and repetitive and requires emotional resilience.
A common path is: start as an apprentice, learn machine tending, manage batches independently, lead a line, then become a store manager or move into equipment maintenance.
This work suits steady, resilient people who can sit or stand for long periods. If getting garments fully clean feels like a worthwhile standard, the field can be stable.
Laundry and dry-cleaning workers sort garments by fabric, operate laundry and dry-cleaning equipment, remove stains, and press items while protecting cleanliness and garment condition.

paragraphs: Early in the morning, sort loads and choose programs by fabric. Spend the morning washing and treating stains, then press, finish, inspect, and package items in the afternoon. Peak periods run continuously, with equipment cleaning handled along the way.
In short, they clean and care for soiled garments. They sort, wash, remove stains, press, inspect, and clean equipment, combining hands-on work with visual judgment as garment-care specialists.

U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data show about 202,600 laundry and dry-cleaning workers employed in 2024, projected to reach 213,500 by 2034. That is a net increase of about 10,900 jobs, with roughly 31,900 annual openings. Median annual pay is about $33,800 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace laundry workers, but it will reduce standard tasks. Automated washing and sorting accelerate routine work, shifting workers from repeated washing toward fabric identification, stain removal, and delicate care. Standard-only washing roles face pressure, while people skilled in stain removal and fabric care become more valuable.
